name: Copper peptide scalp serum
lead: A copper peptide scalp serum is a topical product containing GHK-Cu (copper tripeptide-1), a complex of the tripeptide glycyl-L-histidyl-L-lysine and copper(II), applied to the scalp with the aim of a fuller, thicker-looking head of hair.[1] People use it as an add-on to other hair routines, hoping it supports the follicle environment so hair looks denser.

GHK-Cu occurs naturally in human plasma, saliva and urine, and was isolated from plasma by Loren Pickart in 1973.[1] Its serum level is reported to fall from about 200 ng/ml at age 20 to about 80 ng/ml by age 60.[8] A 2018 review lists increased hair growth and thicker hair among reported effects, alongside collagen and blood vessel stimulation, and notes GHK-Cu is widely used in skin and hair products.[2][9]

Most of the evidence for GHK-Cu comes from cell and animal work and from skin studies such as one randomised trial on CO2 laser-resurfaced skin.[1][7] Reviews of topical GHK note that published data on skin permeability and effectiveness are limited.[3][6] No clinical trial of a copper peptide scalp serum for hair loss was identified.
infobox: About 200 ng/ml at age 20, about 80 ng/ml at age 60 [8]

paras: GHK-Cu is a naturally occurring tripeptide bound to copper. It is proposed to modulate wound healing, attract immune cells, act as an antioxidant and anti-inflammatory, and stimulate collagen and glycosaminoglycan synthesis in skin fibroblasts and blood vessel growth.[1] Scalp serums apply the same ingredient to the scalp, often alongside other topical hair products.

Reviews describe GHK as stimulating blood vessel and nerve outgrowth, increasing collagen, elastin and glycosaminoglycan synthesis, supporting dermal fibroblasts, and showing anti-inflammatory and antioxidant actions.[2] Gene-expression data are cited as explaining how one small molecule could influence many pathways.[2] Proponents extend these actions to the hair follicle, whose size and blood supply are linked to hair thickness.[9]

A 2025 review of topical GHK as an anti-wrinkle peptide says GHK-Cu and its palmitoylated derivative are widely used in cosmetics, but that published information on skin permeability and effectiveness is insufficient.[3] A 2025 review of liposome-encapsulated GHK-Cu says free GHK-Cu is fairly hydrophilic with limited penetration through the outer skin layer, and that liposomes may improve it.[6]
Pickart isolated the copper-binding peptide from human plasma albumin in 1973, and in 1977 the growth-modulating peptide was identified as glycyl-L-histidyl-L-lysine.[1]

No studies found on copper peptide scalp serums for hair loss. Related human work includes a randomised trial of copper tripeptide complex skin care after CO2 laser resurfacing,[7] and reviews of GHK for skin ageing describing small, short studies.[3][8] A 2026 sports-medicine review of peptide therapies including GHK-Cu says rigorous human safety data are scarce for many unapproved peptides.[4] The same reference that records GHK-Cu raising matrix metalloproteinases, which break down dermal proteins, notes more research is needed.[1]

Copper peptide serums are discussed in hair-loss communities as an add-on to minoxidil or finasteride routines. An early T Nation thread (2003) asked whether anyone had used a copper peptide hair product, Folligen being named, to thicken fine hair gained with Rogaine and spironolactone, and wondered why wider acceptance had not followed.[10]

On looksmax.org, GHK-Cu is discussed mainly for skin: members ask whether it can reduce fine lines or calm atopic dermatitis, compare it with Matrixyl, and debate it against other skin options.[11][12][13]

timeline.event: Pickart isolates the copper-binding peptide from human plasma.[1]
The peptide is identified as glycyl-L-histidyl-L-lysine.[1]

lore.intro: Copper peptides are discussed in hair-loss forums as an extra to established treatments, and on looksmax.org mostly as a skin product.[10][11]

claims.claim: GHK-Cu thickens hair and enlarges follicles.
claims.believers: Proponents cite the peptide's reported effects on follicle size and thickness and its presence in many hair products; a 2003 T Nation poster found the theory 'sounds good'.[2][10]
claims.experts: The 2018 review lists the effect among reported actions without a cited trial for it, and no published trial of a scalp serum was found.[2]

claims.claim: GHK-Cu can reduce fine lines and calm skin inflammation.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org user asked about it for fine lines and atopic dermatitis because of its reported anti-inflammatory properties.[11]
claims.experts: Reviews describe collagen-stimulating and wound-healing actions mostly from lab data, with small, short facial studies and limited permeability data.[3][8]

claims.claim: GHK-Cu works better than Matrixyl or other peptides.
claims.believers: Members compare GHK-Cu with Matrixyl as a skin option.[13]
claims.experts: No published studies were found comparing the two.

card.summary: GHK-Cu peptide serum for the scalp: popular in hair stacks, with no published scalp trials behind it.
card.note: Skin evidence is small and short; no scalp hair trials found.

quick.overview:
Copper peptide scalp serums put GHK-Cu, a small copper-binding peptide found naturally in the body, on the scalp. They are marketed for hair thickness and loss prevention.

Most GHK-Cu research is in cell and animal studies, with a few small facial-skin studies. No scalp hair-loss trials were found.
quick.mechanism: Proposed actions include supporting wound healing, antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects, and stimulating collagen and blood vessel growth; none of these have been shown for hair in published human trials.
quick.risks: Sold as a cosmetic ingredient. The source notes GHK-Cu also raises matrix metalloproteinases and advises caution; scalp-specific safety data are not available.

angle.text: Users apply the serum to the scalp as a supplement to routines such as minoxidil or finasteride, with the aim of thicker, denser-looking hair. Its proposed actions are drawn from general GHK-Cu research on skin and wound healing.
